summary:
North Sumatra stands under Indonesia's national framework. The penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment; because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, the provision reaches all consensual same-sex relations, and reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

North Sumatra is not among the two provinces whose own law criminalises same-sex sexual activity between men and between women. Those provisions sit in Aceh and South Sumatra, alongside national morality provisions. Aceh's punishments are imposed under provincial religious law and apply to anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors; two men were publicly caned there for a same-sex relationship in February 2025.

OutRight Action International's 2022 mapping of Indonesia's national laws and discriminatory regional regulations includes North Sumatra among its focus provinces and finds significant regional variation in dress codes, curfews and restrictions on where transgender people may appear. The report states that its findings hold for regions beyond the focus set, so a trans visitor should expect provincial-level rules over presentation and movement rather than a uniform national standard. The specific text of any North Sumatra regulation is not reproduced in the available inventory.

Physical risk is rising nationally. Vigilante mobs are attacking transgender people, and reporting in August 2026 ties the surge to officials' public condemnations and to a presidential decree of October 2025 that lists LGBTQ+ people as a non-military national threat alongside separatism and terrorism. Police raids on LGBT gatherings continue: on 22 June 2025 officers raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after reports of a 'gay party' and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman. Amnesty International said the gathering violated no law and called the operation a blatant violation of human rights and privacy.

Custody has proved lethal for a trans traveller. In August 2022 Rodrigo Ventocilla, a Harvard student on honeymoon in Bali, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges; during a WhatsApp call his mother in Lima was told authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody and his mother alleges police beat him. Indonesian police denied that violence was used.

Expression is criminalised in ways a visitor can trigger. The 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction punishes any writing or audio-visual presentation showing or suggesting same-sex relations with up to seven years' imprisonment. In March 2016 the national broadcasting commission banned television and radio programmes presenting LGBTQ behaviour as normal, the government has blocked websites and apps carrying 'gay' or LGBTQ-related words including Grindr, and a bill to prohibit online content presenting lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender behaviour was under discussion in 2025.

Indonesia recognises only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors, with no third-gender or X option, and legal gender recognition requires sex reassignment surgery and a judge's approval. No national law protects people from discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.

The one documented legal-process case in North Sumatra is favourable. Dimas Cahya, a transgender man from Medan, became the first transgender man in the city to change his name legally to match his identity; after a six-week process the Medan District Court granted the application. The judge warned that the change would 'erase my identity' but otherwise stayed out of LGBTI issues, and the available reporting records no enforcement action against him or his partner as a result of the case.
tangentialFactors:
The provincial layer and the national layer do not move together. North Sumatra carries no provincial criminalisation of same-sex conduct, while Aceh and South Sumatra do; the outward-facing risk in North Sumatra instead runs through dress and appearance rules, mob violence and national police operations rather than through a local sodomy-style offence.

OutRight Action International's mapping covers eight focus provinces and reports both substantial overlap between national and regional rules and significant regional variation in how transgender people are restricted in dress, curfew and presence. The authors state the findings are valid for regions outside the focus set, which places North Sumatra inside a wider pattern of sub-national regulation rather than isolating it.

The Medan name-change case contrasts with the country's rigid formal requirements. National law conditions legal gender recognition on sex reassignment surgery and judicial approval, yet the documented North Sumatra proceeding was resolved in six weeks on a name application, with the presiding judge confining his objection to a remark rather than refusing relief.
localsOnly:
Residents of North Sumatra face dress codes, curfews and restrictions on where transgender people may appear that vary by region rather than following a single national template; the 2022 OutRight mapping names North Sumatra among its focus provinces but the inventory does not reproduce the wording of the applicable local regulation.

Local legal infrastructure exists. A legal-aid organisation in Medan assisted with a transgender man's name-change application, although it put invasive questions to the applicant and his partner before taking the case. The Medan District Court then granted the application in six weeks, making the applicant the first transgender man in the city to change his name legally.

Medan's social climate is described as conservative, with LGBTI people deemed immoral. The judge handling the name change warned that it would 'erase my identity' while declining to engage wider LGBTI issues in the ruling.

Residents have no statutory recourse on grounds of gender identity or sexual orientation: no national law protects people from discrimination or harassment on those grounds, and identity documents carry only 'male' or 'female' descriptors with legal recognition contingent on sex reassignment surgery and a judge's approval.
